title: Financing Contingencies: A Practical Guide for Agents
description: The financing contingency protects buyers but can weaken an offer. How agents can structure it wisely and what to confirm with the loan officer first.
image_alt: Two business people reviewing documents together

faq.q: What does a financing contingency do?
faq.a: It lets a buyer cancel the purchase without losing their deposit if they can't obtain the loan described in the contract within the contingency period.

faq.q: Should a buyer ever waive the loan contingency?
faq.a: Only with a clear understanding of the risk, ideally after a full underwriting review and with a backup plan. It's a decision for the buyer to make with their agent, and possibly an attorney.

faq.q: How long should the loan contingency period be?
faq.a: Long enough for the lender to reach a solid approval, including appraisal. Ask the loan officer what's realistic for that specific file before writing the offer.

body_html:
The financing contingency is one of the most important protections in a purchase contract, and one of the most misunderstood. Write it too loose and your offer looks weak. Write it too tight, or waive it casually, and your client's deposit is exposed. Here's how I'd think about it from the lending side.

What the contingency actually protects

A financing, or loan, contingency gives the buyer the right to cancel without forfeiting their deposit if they can't get the loan described in the contract within a set period. In California, the standard purchase agreement treats the loan and appraisal contingencies separately, and each has its own timeline that can be shortened, lengthened, or removed.

The key phrase is "the loan described in the contract." If the contract says one loan type and amount and the buyer later switches programs, the protection may not line up with reality anymore.

Before you write the offer: four calls worth making

  1. Confirm the pre-approval is real. Were documents reviewed and credit pulled? My post on pre-qualification vs. pre-approval covers what to ask.
  2. Ask what the timeline really is. How quickly can this lender get to underwriting approval for this borrower and this property type?
  3. Discuss appraisal risk. If the price is aggressive relative to comps, plan for it now.
  4. Check property-specific issues. Condos, unpermitted additions, and unique properties can add steps.

Structuring a strong but safe contingency

ApproachWhen it worksWatch out for
Standard contingency periodTypical files with no special issuesCan look less competitive in multiple offers
Shortened contingencyFully documented borrower, fast lender, clean propertyLeaves little room for surprises
Underwritten approval before offerBuyers who want near-cash strengthRequires time and documents up front
Waived contingencyBuyers with substantial resources and backup fundsDeposit at risk if the loan fails

The appraisal is part of the picture

Even when the loan contingency is shortened, the appraisal can still create a gap between price and value. Some buyers add appraisal gap language to show sellers they can cover a shortfall. That's a strategy that needs real cash behind it. I go deeper in this post on appraisal gaps.

Removing contingencies on time

In California, contingencies typically need to be removed in writing. Coordinate with your loan officer before the deadline so your client isn't removing protection before the loan is actually ready. A quick status call two or three days before the removal date is cheap insurance.

The best contingency strategy is the one your client fully understands before they sign.

When a buyer wants to waive the contingency

In multiple-offer situations, buyers sometimes ask about waiving the loan contingency entirely. That decision belongs to the buyer, but it should be an informed one. Before a buyer waives, I'd want to confirm a few things:

  • The file has been fully reviewed, ideally by an underwriter, not just pre-approved
  • The buyer understands the deposit is at risk if the loan doesn't fund for any reason
  • There's a backup plan, such as additional assets or an alternative lender
  • The appraisal risk is understood separately, since waiving one contingency doesn't eliminate the other risk

Some buyers take a middle path: a short contingency period paired with a fully underwritten approval. That signals strength to the seller while keeping some protection. It's often the best of both worlds.

Communicating loan strength to the listing agent

A strong financing section in an offer is more than the contingency length. Listing agents look for clues about reliability. A short note in the offer package about the loan program, the status of the approval, and the loan officer's direct contact information helps. A quick call from the loan officer to the listing agent helps even more. The goal is simple: make the seller confident the deal will close.

The takeaway

A financing contingency should match the strength of the actual loan file, not just the pressure of the market. Talk to the loan officer before you write, structure timelines around real underwriting speed, and remove contingencies only when the loan is truly there. Agents who work this way win offers without putting deposits at risk.
